This can be accomplished through anticipatory guidance, surveillance, screening and brief interventions, and done in ways that are trauma-informed, equitable and free of bias. The report also highlights the value of collaboration with integrated health providers, schools and communities. Learn more about the report in AAP News: https://bit.ly/4urxCsm

A recent piece in Pediatrics shares why vitamin K refusal should be treated as a high-risk perinatal safety event, requiring education about the potentially life-threatening consequences of this decision. The piece offers guidance for pediatricians on explaining the risks of refusal and the injection’s potentially life-saving benefits. Learn more about the importance of vitamin K: https://bit.ly/4d2lXKt

Amid concerns about a physician shortage, AAP President Dr. Racine cautiously applauded a recent federal policy reversal that now exempts physicians from a freeze on processing visas from certain countries. Though questions still remain. Earlier this year, federal officials suspended visa processing for people from 39 countries, citing security concerns. However, the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services updated its website late last week to say the holds have been lifted for medical physicians. Read the full piece in AAP News: https://bit.ly/4dqWSZO

May is Mental Health Awareness Month, and AAP has released a new clinical report with guidance for pediatricians on approaching mental health and emotional development. The goals of #MentalHealthAwarenessMonth are to reduce associated stigma, provide education and encourage access to care. The AAP report outlines how pediatricians can support families by taking a broad approach to a child’s emotional health rather than waiting until challenges arise or diagnosing and treating discrete conditions or disorders only. The clinical report provides a stepped approach that may be helpful for addressing mental and emotional health concerns in pediatrics and acknowledges that advocacy is needed to expand mental and emotional resources widely. Learn more about the report: https://bit.ly/4urxCsm

In an AAP Voices blog, Pediatrician William Dietz shared several stories he learned about polio while speaking with residents of a retirement community. These stories served as an important reminder: the human costs of polio have not been fully forgotten... “Most of these residents - and myself at 81 - were the last generation in the U.S. to suffer from poliomyelitis, and the first generation to benefit from the development of the polio vaccine,” said Dr. Dietz. “...I believe this experience comes with a special obligation to convey the debilitating consequences of this infection and its impacts.” Read more from Dr. Dietz about the importance of the polio vaccine: https://bit.ly/3PaN6BX

Pediatricians recently spoke with The Cut about the increase in vaccine hesitancy they are seeing in their practice. Swipe to see what pediatricians around the country are seeing, and read the full piece here: https://bit.ly/4whUn3I

Emergency department (ED) visits for tick bites are the highest in at least a decade, according to CDC data when comparing this time of year to past seasons. Children under the age of 10 have the highest rates of ED visits for tick bites this year. Ticks can cause serious diseases like Lyme disease, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, and alpha-gal syndrome. People can protect themselves from tick bites by wearing EPA-registered insect repellent and permethrin-treated clothing, checking for ticks after spending time outdoors and removing them quickly. Learn more in AAP News: https://bit.ly/4sW2KPt

The measles virus can impact children’s immune systems, and not in a good way. The measles virus can wipe out immune memory of other harmful viruses and bacteria. This side effect, known as immune amnesia, can affect anyone who gets measles. Measles knows how to find and get rid of the helpful memory cells, and can erase up to 73% of your child's immune memory. When some or all of the memory cells are gone, it is harder for your child's immune system to remember germs and fight off infections. Your child will have immunity to measles, but their immunity to other diseases will be lower. Vaccines and new infections are the only way to get this immunity back. To keep your child's immune system strong and protect against potentially serious infections, the AAP recommends the measles, mumps, rubella (MMR) vaccine series. https://bit.ly/4vYD9bh

South Carolina’s measles outbreak has ended after nearly 1,000 cases including 21 hospitalizations. Of the 997 cases reported since late September 2025, about 91% were among children and teens. Just over 97% of cases were among people who were not fully vaccinated or had an unknown vaccination status. The state was able to declare the outbreak over after 42 days without a new case. Thousands of measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine doses were administered during the outbreak. Doses increased 94% in Spartanburg County and 82% in the Upstate region compared to the same time period a year earlier. But risks of additional outbreaks remain in areas with low vaccination rates. The AAP continues to recommend a two-dose MMR vaccination series to ensure children are protected from measles. Read the full piece in AAP News: https://bit.ly/422vTxl

Disrupted caregiving can sometimes lead to child abuse and neglect and significantly impair a child’s emotional regulation and development. Early recognition and support of disrupted caregivers can lead to better outcomes for children. Pediatricians can reframe childhood behavior concerns and identify opportunities for supportive, preventive intervention. The 3 Rs (Reassure, Return to Routine and Regulate) provide a framework to help families navigate challenging times. Learn more: https://bit.ly/3TltFpJ

In a recent opinion piece for The Salt Lake Tribune, four pediatricians describe how fear-based immigration policies are making it increasingly difficult for children in immigrant families to access essential medical care. When families are afraid to seek the care they need, kids miss checkups, vaccinations, and treatment – putting their health at risk. These pediatricians are calling for a shift in how we approach immigration policy, emphasizing that policies shaped by fear can have serious consequences for children. Read the full piece: https://bit.ly/48p1XPM

As a mom and an emergency medicine physician, Dr. BeachGem knows every parent wants to make the best decision for their child. That’s why she recommends that her patients follow the AAP’s childhood immunization schedule. AAP recommendations are backed by decades of scientific evidence and provide kids with the strongest protection against preventable diseases. Hear more about the vaccine recommendations this #WorldImmunizationWeek:

Rotavirus spreads easily and can cause severe diarrhea and dehydration. And with cases rising across the country, it’s important that infants and children are up to date on their rotavirus vaccine series so their immune systems can build resistance to the virus. Read more about the rise in rotavirus cases from NBC News: https://nbcnews.to/4eGyfcI

With more parents refusing the vitamin K shot for newborns, education on why the shot is so important has never been more critical. Babies who don’t receive the vitamin K shot are 81 times more likely to develop Vitamin K Deficiency Bleeding, which can be deadly to infants. Pediatricians play an important role in partnering with parents to make the best decisions for their children. A recent Pediatrics article highlights the steps pediatricians can take the educate and inform parents on the importance of vitamin K. Read the piece: https://bit.ly/4d2lXKt

Pediatricians are seeing increased hesitancy among parents when it comes to the vitamin K birth shot, a critical aspect of routine newborn care that protects babies from dangerous bleeding, known as Vitamin K Deficiency Bleeding. The injection gives babies the vitamin K they need until they can start getting it from solid food and making it themselves. The AAP continues to recommend that all newborns receive the vitamin K shot at birth. Learn more in this Healthy Children article. #NationalInfantImmunizationWeek https://bit.ly/3UxLRff

Measles cases continue to climb this year, as the outbreak has impacted 32 states with 72% of cases among children and teens. Case counts this year have been the highest in South Carolina, Utah, Texas and Florida, according to CDC data. Attention is turning to Utah where an outbreak that began in June 2025 has produced over 600 cases. When the vaccination rate is more than 95%, most people are protected through community immunity, according to the CDC. However, just under 89% of Utah kindergartners in the 2024-’25 school year were vaccinated. The AAP recommends ensuring patients are covered with a two-dose measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccination series. Read the full story in AAP News: https://bit.ly/41LBUyv

In South Carolina and across the country, ongoing measles outbreaks continue to put one of our most vulnerable populations – babies too young to be vaccinated – at risk. Measles can cause severe illness in young babies, like pneumonia and brain swelling, and can even cause them to stop eating and drinking. The best way to protect babies from measles is through community immunity, which is achieved when at least 95% of a community is vaccinated. But unfortunately, declining vaccination rates are eroding this protection. Read more about the ongoing measles outbreak and the risks the disease poses to babies in Associated Press. https://bit.ly/4tm3b6A

This #NationalInfantImmunizationWeek, the AAP is highlighting the importance of the hepatitis B vaccine at birth. Hepatitis B is a serious liver infection that can be passed from mother to baby at birth. But because of the vaccine, it’s preventable. The first dose of the hepatitis B vaccine is recommended within 24 hours of birth, giving infants a strong start toward lifelong protection. Pediatricians can answer questions parents have about the hepatitis B vaccine series. https://bit.ly/4iyUYYhhttps://bit.ly/4iyUYYh

We are devastated by this weekend’s shooting in Louisiana that claimed the lives of eight children. While details continue to emerge, what remains tragically clear is the unacceptable toll that gun violence continues to take on children, families, and communities across the country. Firearm injuries are the leading cause of death for children and teens in the United States. This is a public health epidemic that is injuring and killing young people at alarming rates, leaving lasting trauma for survivors and unimaginable loss to so many families. Gun violence is a direct threat to the health and safety of children and teens everywhere. The AAP and pediatricians remain committed to advocating for the policies needed to protect children and to end gun violence.

Utah is the latest state to be significantly impacted by the measles outbreak, with nearly 600 people (mostly children) reported sick, according to a New York Times report. Vaccination rates need to be above about 95% for communities to achieve community immunity and limit the spread of measles. Yet, reporting shows that in the 2024-25 school year, about 11% of kindergartners in Utah had exemptions or were missing documentation to show they were vaccinated against measles. Previously, the exemption rate was closer to 7%, signaling a troubling increase. The AAP recommends children receive the two-dose measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccination series to protect them from measles. Read the full piece: https://nyti.ms/3OI0Dkd

AAP joined two dozen medical groups in urging federal officials to expedite immigration proceedings for international medical graduates (IMGs) in the United States. Read more about the letter in AAP News: https://bit.ly/4tki9tZ

March is almost in the books! We are just two days away from Autism Awareness Month. This year we have a trifecta of events to celebrate and raise public awareness and acceptance for those afflictes with this lifelong disorder. Kathleen is not one of those super-high functioning autistic individuals like the ones you see on TV that become doctors at the age of sixteen. In fact, Kathleen is pretty much the opposite. Kathleen struggles every day. She will never be able to take care of herself and relies on us to help her with the most simple tasks for neurotypical individuals. Thank God she was blessed with the most beautiful mother of all time, Jackie, who has given up her own life to make sure Kath feels safe and comfortable and who cares for her from the time her eyes open until they close in exhaustion. Kathleen doesn't know the concept of "Autism Awareness". She only knows that she is loved to infinity by us and literally, that's all she needs. But Jackie and I surely understand how important it is for us to create as much awareness and acceptance for Kathleen before we leave her alone in this cruel world. With that being said, for parents of profoundly autistic adults and children, Autism Awareness Month is something to look forward to. I live at 107 Locust Avenue in Neptune City. In the 70's and early '80s, the Philadelphia Flyers were known as the Broad Street Bullies because they were ruthless, abrasive and unapologetically obnoxious. Well it's 2025 now and we have our own version of these bullies right on our own street. Let's call them the Locust Avenue Assholes. They live at 112 Locust Avenue and rent out the house directly across the street from us (106) where their parents lived prior to their demise. It is well known on our street, that this one particular family seems to think they own the taxpayer-funded thoroughfare. We've lived on the street for nearly 30 years and since day one they've been nothing but nasty to us and to every other neighbor to which I've spoken. They have a series of at least five automobiles, many of them commercial-type vans and trucks used for construction and landscape businesses. For some reason they think they are entitled to the park their vehicles wherever they want. Meanwhile, if someone parks in front of one of the two houses that they own on the street, they literally walk up to the people and tell them they have to move their car and or truck. Today, my landscapers who have been there every week since April, parked directly across the street from me in front of one of their houses. They were there to do a fall cleanup getting rid of the leaves sprucing up the property prior to us putting up our Christmas decorations. At the sight of this, the father of said tribe of deplorable individuals, approached the landscapers and told them that they had to move their truck. The truck was parked legally, it was going to be there for a short time, and it was not blocking any driveway or causing any problem. The landscapers did move their truck, but as they worked, this gentleman chose to videotape them on his phone...for what reason I don't know. Now let me tell you, these people don't necessarily care about anybody's color race or creed. They simply hate everyone. But something tells me that these people probably hate Latino people to an even greater degree because their son owns a competing landscaping business. This nonsense has been going on for the 28 plus years that we have lived on the street. People that are attending parties at my house have been asked to move their cars. My car was called in to the police as an "abandoned vehicle" because it was moved from its normal spot right in front of our house, to a spot literally 50 yards north on the same side of the street not in front of anyone's house. However, that spot is where they park their commercial vehicles. The police knocked on my door on a Saturday morning at 8:30 a.m. upsetting my severely autistic daughter which,in turn, ruined an entire day. Since it's Thanksgiving, I'd like to thank Jesus for putting people like them in our lives. They are a constant reminder of what not to be. Yet they are a reminder of the teaching of Jesus, that when someone slaps you on the cheek, don't retaliate, turn the other cheek and let them smack that one as well. I hope my neighbors on Locust Avenue and throughout the town read this post and, if they want to do something peacefully to punish these bullies, they stop using the landscaping company that they own. Hitting someone in the pocketbook and the wallet easy. We've been living with these assholes for 28 years now, and although they try to break us, they won't succeed because we have righteousness on our side. This post is shareable to all. On behalf of Autism New Jersey we would like to thank the nine store NJ Division of Wegmans for their donation of 5000.00 in support of Autism Acceptance Month. Having worked for this phenomenal company for over twenty years, I can say that they adhere strictly to the standards that I learned at orientation so many years ago. At Wegmans, you learn that the Acronym MERCH is a standard, not only to work by, but to live by as well. M stands for Making a Difference (in the lives of others and the community at large) E stands for Empowerment (in the decision-making process making sure that they stand by their team members) R stands for Respect (all team members are respective of each other and our customers without bias) C stands for Caring (we are encouraged to care about each other, our customers and the municipalities in which we work) H stands for High Standards (team members provide the best standard of service that we can while also making sure the products sold and the experience of our customers in our store are met with these very same standards. Wegmans employs many individuals who have special needs, many of whom I have had the pleasure of working with at both the Wegmans (Manalapan) and Wegmans (Ocean) stores. Having a daughter with Autism this shows me just what a phenomenal company for which I work. When I'm not working or going in for the late shift we like to bring Kathleen into the Ocean store where we do three loops pushing her in her chair. In those three loops we are greeted with smiles and hellos from almost every single coworker of mine. Kathleen does have her favorites however. She likes to wish my Pharmacy coworkers "good morning" as we start our loop. Then we move into the GM section where we see her friends Gerald and Maryanne. As we head to the dairy we get to see the always smiling Gail Grim Marino who greets us with a "Hi Kelly Family". Sometimes we get to see Samantha Castardi Williams as well. As we proceed past the cheese departments we get to see Bianca Rivero and all the people working hard. Then onto the meat department where we see Harold Kelley, Tom Boyle and all the other smiling faces. In Fish, we get to see Craig, Yen and Doreen among so many others. Then to prepared where Ryan, Mary Ellen Kary, Rob, Michael, Gina, Carlos, Lauren, Joe and all the others who are hard at work make sure to give us a wave. Next we go past subs and pizza where Donna rings a bell to make Kathleen smile and Jasmine Alston provides us with a smile and another "good morning" We also see Joan Marie and Kerry who are so happy to see us. Finally we go through bakery where we get to see Jodi Madigan, Aurelia, Casey and all the people covered in flour. Then we get to produce where we are once again greeted with smiles and then past the cashiers where Kaitlyn Hughes, Kathy, Mike, Michael, Rosemary Henehan Viglone and so many more wish us a great day. Finally, we finish the loop with a visit to HBC where we see Mary Jo Binns, Joan, Terry, and Lynne Langbein. Then it's off to do loop number two! There are so many more that I failed to mention but this would be as long as "War and Peace" lol. We are so thankful for the way that these people treat Kathleen as we do these three loops. Kathleen doesn't respond often with words unless we prompt her but we know by her smile that she feels so good when these people show her, and us, such simple acts of kindness and understanding. I would be remiss if I didn't thank the wonderful Managerial Staff, Jenny, Jimmy, Jackie, and Tara who also are always there to greet us with a genuine smile. When we start our day at Wegmans doing these "loops" it makes us feel what is truly meant by the promotion of "Autism Acceptance and Awareness". When we are with Kath at Wegmans we feel safe and secure and our minds are at ease as Kath is allowed to be herself and loved for being so. So, in closing, thank you again to this wonderful organization. From the corporate offices, to the division offices, to the store managers on down the line it is a company that truly cares about those who work for it. I am thankful, humbled and proud to be a member of the Wegmans family!

Jackie and I have a great amount of gratitude and love in our hearts for all the people who have supported our mission of over 20 years. As I've stated before, we will do just about anything to promote acceptance and understanding for Kathleen and all God's special children. Jackie started this whole beautiful thing when we received help from Autism New Jersey when we were struggling to get Kathleen the services that these children so deeply deserve. They helped us and we wanted to give them back. I remember the night when I sent out about 20 requests for an online funding drive for the organization. Within 2 days we had 1500.00 in pledges. That felt really good so Jackie then talked me into a little annual function of 300 plus friends and family called "The Autism Awareness Gift Auction". Over ten years that event raised over 200,000.00 for ANJ. It was a lot of hard work but it was a labor of love that we undertook as a committee of two. When Covid hit, we had to put that event on hold. It truly left a hole in our hearts. Thankfully we had developed a great relationship with the Fitzsimmons family and we were able to work with them to put together the Annual Autism Awareness Day at Patrick's Grille when everything started opening back up. Every time you enter the room announce yourself. “Hi- it’s ………...” NEVER ask- Do you know who I am??? That causes anxiety. 2. If I get dementia, I want my friends and family to embrace my reality. 🌸 3. If I think my dead friend is still alive, or if I think we’re visiting my parents for dinner, let me believe those things. I’ll be much happier for it.❤️ 4. If I get dementia, don’t argue with me about what is true for me versus what is true for you.👍🏽❤️👍🏽 5. If I get dementia, and I am not sure who you are, do not take it personally. My timeline is confusing to me.👍🏽👍🏽👍🏽 6. If I get dementia and can no longer use utensils, do not start feeding me. Instead, switch me to a finger-food diet, and see if I can still feed myself.❤️🥰❤️🥰 7. If I get dementia, and I am sad or anxious, hold my hand and listen. If I get dementia, I still want to enjoy the things that I’ve always enjoyed. Help me find a way to exercise, read, and visit with friends. ❤️ 10. If I get dementia, ask me to tell you a story from my past. 11. If I get dementia, and I become agitated, take the time to figure out what is bothering me. ❤️ 12. DEPRESSION TIPS: Shower. Not a bath, a shower. Use water as hot or cold as you like. You don’t even need to wash. Just get in under the water and let it run over you for a while. Sit on the floor if you need to. Moisturize everything. Use whatever lotion you like. Unscented? Dollar store lotion? Fancy 48 hour lotion that makes you smell like a field of wildflowers? Use whatever you want, and use it all over your entire skin. Put on clean, comfortable clothes. Put on your favorite underwear. Those ridiculous boxers you bought last christmas with candy cane hearts on the butt? Put them on. Drink cold water. Use ice. If you want, add some mint or lemon for an extra boost. Clean something. Doesn’t have to be anything big. Organize one drawer of a desk. Wash five dirty dishes. Do a load of laundry. Scrub the bathroom sink. Blast music. Listen to something upbeat and dancey and loud, something that’s got lots of energy. Sing to it, dance to it, even if you suck at both. Make food. Don’t just grab a granola bar to munch. Take the time and make food. Even if it’s ramen. Add something special to it, like a soft boiled egg or some veggies. Prepare food, it tastes way better, and you’ll feel like you accomplished something. Make something. Write a short story or a poem, draw a picture, color a picture, fold origami, crochet or knit, sculpt something out of clay, anything artistic. Even if you don’t think you’re good at it. Create. Go outside. Take a walk. Sit in the grass. Look at the clouds. Smell flowers. Put your hands in the dirt and feel the soil against your skin. Call someone. Call a loved one, a friend, a family member, call a chat service if you have no one else to call. Talk to a stranger on the street. Have a conversation and listen to someone’s voice. If you can’t bring yourself to call, text or email or whatever, just have some social interaction with another person. Even if you don’t say much, listen to them. It helps. Cuddle your pets if you have them/can cuddle them. Take pictures of them. Talk to them. Tell them how you feel, about your favorite movie, a new game coming out, anything. May seem small or silly to some, but this list keeps people alive. *** At your absolute best you won’t be good enough for the wrong people. But at your worst, you’ll still be worth it to the right ones. Remember that. Keep holding on. *** In case nobody has told you today I love you and you are worth your weight and then some in gold, so be kind to yourself and most of all keep pushing on!!!! Everyday hero's. ... and yet another Hero Officer. New Jersey State Police Recently, we received this letter from a passing motorist who witnessed Trooper Jamarr Morris helping a little boy and his two dogs on the Garden State Parkway: I am writing this letter to inform you of an incident that took place on the southbound side of the New Jersey Garden State Parkway on Monday, August 23 at approximately 2:45 PM in the area of mile marker 112. I was driving home from work. I am a new commuter, and being so new I have become very cognizant of the deer that roam the side of the parkway no matter the time. I try to remain vigilant to their whereabouts, as I know they pose quite a threat of accident. On this particular day I noticed two dogs and their 8 year old owner running in tow in the woods where these deer typically feed. They were headed directly for the parkway. I had an immediate pit in my stomach! As both a mother and educator, I anticipated that if these dogs ran onto the GSP that the little boy would be quick to follow. And that is exactly what happened! I along with two other motorists slowed the traffic to a dead stop, I know...not the easiest decision to make, nor the best! But the crisis I foresaw was too grim to imagine any other way. Fortunately Officer Jamar Morris (car 204) was only about 1.5 miles ahead. I believe he was on a recent traffic stop. He must have noticed that the traffic was not moving and he safely turned his vehicle around and returned to the scene which included two loose dogs running all over the GSP, one 8 year old boy who seemed to be in shock who was chasing them, and 5 patient adults who had stopped the traffic and were trying their best to render aid. Officer Morris quickly and calmly took control of the scene. The young boy was able to only capture one dog. He only had one leash. Officer Morris grabbed the other dog and carried him. I am not sure he even liked dogs. He took the young man to the Trooper vehicle. I could hear him asking the young boy where he lived and what had happened. He scooped them all into the vehicle and safely moved over to the side of the road. The whole incident took less than 5 minutes. As Officer Morris passed my vehicle all I could say to him was "YOU ARE A HERO!" And maybe we were all heroes that day, right down to the little boy who just didn't want to lose his dogs. But this was Officer Morris's scene that day! He took charge of what could have been an incredible tragedy on the Garden State Parkway. That young boy and his pups all put their heads on the pillow safely that night, as did we all! Life never prepares us for these types of days! We all just lead with our hearts and calmness of mind! As I put my own head on the pillow on that Monday night I really wished I could have had a group hug and a moment with all these individuals. Thank you Trooper Morris, the concerned citizens that stopped to help, and the motorist who shared this story with us.

I told you about the Monaco GP's twisting, undulating circuit. Monaco is built on the side of a mountain. So it's those up-hill-down-dale kind of public roads that the race course uses. ⌛ After concentrating on Monaco recently -- I don't hate it anymore. I've come to look at the track the way I'd look at moguls on a ski slope. ⛷️ Because the circuit constantly undulates, I've been looking for the best places -- the rise in a corner, a pavement change before a corner, a mid-straight bump -- to apply throttle, steering, brake. Work off of the moguls. 🧑🏻‍🩰 I have to read the pavement better. Most race circuits are smooth as glass. Not this one!

I tell ya... nothing's going right, you hang your head, figuring tomorrow's another day. And then you shave 11 whole seconds off one of your personal bests. 🤣🤣🤣 Did La Sarthe today with the BMW Hyper Car. The car that hasn't done much until it recently won the endurance race at Spa, and finished 2nd this past weekend at Detroit! Two diametrically opposed circuits! 🥵 Couldn't get it to do sh**. It hates braking while cornering, and it tended to plow -- which scrubs off speed. So I'm having a frustrating day. 😕 I jump over to the Nürburgring Gesamtstrecke with the Mercedes AMG GT3 to clean the palate. This is the car I struggled with at the Glen. 😮 I'm sloppy. Transitioning from the Hyper Car to the slower, less-responsive GT3 isn't going well, but I relax and figure I'll just get some laps under my belt. Look up at the end, and I shaved ELEVEN SECONDS off my PB with the Merc! What dafuq??? 🤣🤣🤣

This is the ~40mph chicane at Monza -- at the end of the almost 200mph, flat-out front straight. 🚀 And after months, and miles away at other circuits, but coming back to this circuit a fair amount, I finally have a "pretty good" braking point to slow down enough for this corner. Efficiently. ⚓ It's actually too conservative, but it's infinitely better than where I was before! I need to cut things closer. But that will come with time, visualization, and muscle memory. 💪🏼👍🏻

I think of it as a controlled crash. At Monaco -- among the glitterati -- the guardrails are always just centimeters away, the curbs are willing to pitch the car into the guardrails if you even look at them wrong, and the car is exploding around a too-narrow, constantly undulating public road surface. 🎢 I hate the place. 😠 Yet today, I lowered my personal best NINE seconds to a 1:33 in the F2 car. 😳 It's because of all the other hard work I've done over the last few months on all the other different race circuits with all the different types of race cars. It translates. 🏋🏻‍♂️ But it IS kinda neat to blast through one section, just barely keep the car under control and not hitting anything, and then blasting on to the next section. Last day of the GT3 comparison at the Glen. Had to do the Ferrari, Lambo, Corvette, and Porsche for the second time. I need this displayed every time I get into the sim rig! Thanks, guys! 🤣🤣🤣 Drove the last four GT3 cars: McLaren, Porsche, Mustang, Ferrari. I'm amazed again at how completely different these cars drive. But that's the idea. 💡 I've mostly worked on learning the different tracks: the 'Ring, Monza, Monaco, the Glen, Le Mans, Spa, etc.. And though I used a variety of cars, it was really about the tracks. 🤓 Now I've switched my focus to *feeling* the cars more -- trying to absorb their characteristics and find their limits. And eventually, feeling when they're at the limit *BEFORE* they go over the limit! 🤦🏻

On Day 2 of my GT3 car comparison, I drove the Audi R8, the Aston Martin Vantage, and the Mercedes AMG GT. The Audi's handling was stable and benign. Did whatever I wanted it to do. ⚓ Right away I could feel the Aston was nose-heavy. The engine is in front of the driver, but set so far back in the chassis that it's considered a mid-engined car. 🏹 Still, I had to get that massive weight pointed in the right direction to get fast times. And it posted the fastest time of all so far. 🤷🏻 The Merc has that same chassis layout but seemed lighter, had quicker steering, and tended to wander if I didn't purposefully point it. I was 2 seconds slower with it than with all the other cars. ⏳ But this is the car multiple F1 World Champion, Max Verstappen, chooses to race and win with during his downtime. The takeaway? It's possible the other cars shield my weaknesses, and the Merc highlights them. 🤔

My next improvement program with sim racing is to feel and understand the cars better. I've been concentrating on learning the tracks, now I want to better understand the cars. 🔩 Today I drove some of the GT3 category cars at the Glen to compare their different characteristics. Drove the Lexus RC F, the Lamborghini Huracan, the BMW M4, and the Corvette. Tomorrow I'll do the rest: Mercedes, Aston Martin, Ferrari, Mustang, Porsche. 🔧 Kind of eye-opening. 😕 I hated the Corvette because I really had to work to get the front end to grip -- yet I did my fastest time with it. 🤣🤣🤣

I love it when a plan comes together. The best I could do on the 13-mile Nürburgring Nordschleife Tourist circuit with the Porsche 919 hybrid was a 5:39. The record is 5:19, with that same car. 😲 To improve, I decided to turn continuous laps on the 15-mile Gesamtstrecke (Nürburgring Overall Circuit). With the Tourist, there's a start and a finish, and then you have to pull off and stop at the toll booth to go around again. 🤦🏻 First time on the Gesamtstrecke, I did 3 laps and was wasted. But I wanted to work on endurance and concentration, so I gradually built up the number of laps each time. 💪🏻 When I tried the Tourist today, I cut my personal best by SEVEN SECONDS!!! From that 5:39 down to 5:32. Not by working on speed but on concentration and endurance. Funny how that works. 😉

D-Day was the name given to the June 6, 1944, invasion of the beaches at Normandy in northern France by troops from the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom and other countries during World War II. France at the time was occupied by the armies of Nazi Germany, and the amphibious assault—codenamed Operation Overlord—landed some 156,000 Allied soldiers on the beaches of Normandy by the end of the day. Despite their success, some 4,000 Allied troops were killed by German soldiers defending the beaches. At the time, the D-Day invasion was the largest naval, air and land operation in history, and within a few days about 326,000 troops, more than 50,000 vehicles and some 100,000 tons of equipment had landed. By August 1944, all of northern France had been liberated, and in spring of 1945 the Allies had defeated the Germans. Historians often refer to D-Day as the beginning of the end of World War II.

The Cross Still Offends By Pastor Rich Bitterman The bullet tore the air in half. A folding chair rattled. A Bible dropped. A young man slumped sideways beneath a white event tent, eyes wide with the weight of eternity. It was supposed to be a conversation. A “prove me wrong” segment. But this time, rebuttal came not with words, but with a rifle. Charlie Kirk didn’t get to finish his sentence. I got the news just before prayer meeting. I contemplated this death as I prepared to lead the saints in prayer. But I didn’t feel like praying. Not tonight. My hands were still. My mouth was ready. But my soul was pacing. Angry. Grieving. Tempted. Tempted to grow quiet. Tempted to sit this one out. Tempted to wonder if any of this, faith, boldness, public gospel witness, is still worth it. Because hatred in this country isn’t simmering anymore. It is boiling. Europe is trembling. Israel is burning. Rockets lit the sky over Gaza again. And now, here on American soil, the blood of a Christian apologist paints the pavement of a university quad. What do you do with that? What do you say when courage gets gunned down in daylight? Charlie Kirk was no perfect man. None of us are. But he had backbone where most of us don’t anymore. He was a believer. Unashamed. Unafraid. He understood that real conversations only happen when truth is welcome at the table. And the truth he carried most was Christ. He brought the gospel into public space on purpose. Because the gospel isn’t supposed to stay in church basements and private Bible studies. It is meant to confront. It is supposed to offend. It was not made for safety. The Word became flesh and they nailed Him to a tree. So of course they came for Charlie. Of course they reached for a gun. This is what evil does when it runs out of arguments. It doesn’t reason. It kills. That’s the part that catches in my throat. Not just the sadness, but the strategy of hell behind it. The Enemy wants us afraid. He wants us to see what happened to Charlie and backpedal. He wants the rest of us to whisper, to soften the message, to believe the lie that faith should stay private. But Christ never whispered. He preached in temples, on hillsides, in courtrooms, at dinner tables. And when they told Him to be quiet, He picked up His cross. Not a symbolic one. A real one. Heavy. Bloody. Splintered. When Jesus said, “Follow Me,” He didn’t hand out maps. He handed out crosses. That’s what I remembered tonight. I sat in our prayer space, surrounded by saints who had brought prayer lists and worn Bibles. And I realized I didn’t want to lead them in mourning. I wanted to lead them into battle. Not with banners or fists, but with open Bibles and tear-stained prayers. The kind of war that kneels in gravel beside the wounded, hands them living water, and refuses to leave. The kind that speaks both mercy and judgment without flinching. The kind Charlie died for. This world is not a friend to grace. But grace isn’t fragile. “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?” Paul didn’t leave that question unanswered. “Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or sword?” —Romans 8:35 He piles up every fear you and I carry and then sets them on fire. “No. In all these things we are more than conquerors.” That means bullets don’t win. Slander doesn’t win. Prison bars don’t win. Death doesn’t win. You can lose everything in this world and still walk into glory with your head lifted high. Because the love of God in Christ Jesus isn’t suspended by headlines or gunfire. There are two worlds unfolding right now. The one you see. And the one you don’t. One is filled with chaos. The other is filled with crowns. I believe that when Charlie Kirk’s body slumped to the concrete, his soul stood upright in heaven. Not limping. Not silenced. Not stunned. But crowned. He didn’t fall. He crossed. The great cloud of witnesses gained another voice. And I wonder if Stephen met him there. The first martyr. The man who got stoned for preaching what the crowd didn’t want to hear. The man who, in his final breath, saw the heavens open. The only time in all of Scripture we see Jesus standing at the right hand of God, rising to receive one of His own. I like to believe He stood again. Are you afraid? Do you feel the tremble in your spirit? Do you wonder if it’s still worth it to speak boldly, to carry your Bible, to preach the gospel in a world that doesn’t just disagree but wants you gone? You’re not alone. You’re not weak for feeling that. But you are called to something stronger than silence. Don’t let fear become your theology. The cost is high. But the reward? The reward is Christ. And He’s not a concept. He’s a King. Heaven is not empty. It is filled with scarred saints who refused to bow to fear. Men who were stoned. Women who were burned. Children who sang while the flames climbed. And every last one of them arrived. There is no difficulty that can cancel the promise of God. There is no persecution that can derail your destination. There is no sniper’s bullet that can separate a soul from Christ. Your life is not measured by how long you live on earth, but by how much of it was spent pointing to heaven. Paul said, “I have fought the good fight… I have kept the faith.” Then he looked toward the reward. Not a monument. Not a mention in history books. But a crown. Handed to him by the One with nail marks still in His hands. So let me say this clearly. We do not mourn like the world mourns. We do not write eulogies dripping with sentiment. We sing songs of resurrection. We carry the banner of a Kingdom that does not tremble. Charlie Kirk did not die for nothing. He died carrying the same message you and I must now carry forward. The cross stands tall. The tomb is still empty. And the gospel has not lost one ounce of power. So pick up your cross. Wipe your eyes. And keep going. The crown is worth it. The King is coming. And there’s still time to speak. Even if they shoot. Lord, give us courage. And if not safety, give us joy. For we carry not just the message, but the marks. another year ma, thought i had this down, your mom taking you over to the other side.. but not as tough as i thought i was. saw this billy crystal movie, about a writer starting his walk down Alzheimer's road. it was a comedy ... it was not realistic... but some scenes in it... was watching you walk down your dementia road again. but now i knew what was coming.. i should have known more, i should have done more. real tears watching this movie. but we had fun ma... driving to the boardwalk at spring lake with windows and sun roof wide open... or eating pizza at point pleasant on a cold winter Saturday... what was most important.. being there.. holding your hand... the boardwalk was where you grew up in the summers with your mom and siblings.. you told me stories about that time i never heard before. me holding your hand was like being back in Toledo on Perth street before dad had cancer and we walked round the block after dinner. aunt peg, shirley, emily and aimee.. we celebrated your life when you were alive. Emily will be a fine nurse in part because of what you taught her in your final years. that's a fine legacy for you ma. being a survivor may seem like a great idea.. but when you told me that you did not buy Christmas cards anymore... the cost of the being last one standing started to hit. i think you are in a good place now ma... your mom and dad, dad, all your brothers and sisters... all your friends from river dell and texaco... mr timoney and mr grainger... and especially the francels and the kaczala's. they are all with you.. you know who has great stories about you.. who really cared about you... the women who stayed with you. Tonya, Amy, Ita, Anita, Bea, Tea and Comfort... I wish i could have a dinner with them to hear all about you again... aging and dementia was so hard on you... but not anymore.

Good day down at sandy hook yesterday.. best place to go to get second wind after a long tough hot summer. For years it was some combination of aunt peg, mom, Shirley, Aimee and Emily and Tea or Bea or Comfort and me every Saturday at the boardwalk or mom’s house.. mom has moved on to be with her mom an dad and siblings.. but it was a great day for us.. hoping to repeat in October… happy birthday ma!

It’s been a year ma. Miss the 2am phone calls, the hours of driving.. miss walking with you on the boardwalk and sitting outback of your house. The search for the perfect onion rings.. and that search continues.. But dementia was like a thief in the night, taking things here and there. That pill.. ugh. I think you are in a much better place now. With dad, your mom and dad.. all your brothers and sisters and uncle Jim, Uncle Tom, aunt Marion and aunt Mary.. miss them all.. but they can take care of you better than we did. Miss you but all these memories.. you are never far away…

Today was a good day! First family pool day of the season, couldn’t ask for better weather. It started when Amanda & Sean got here just before 1:00. Karen & I were out back on the deck, so they let themselves in. Our 4 year old grandson came walking through the slider from the family room onto the deck and perfectly greeted us with a “Hello” and came to each of us and gave us a big hug. This may not seem like a big deal, but those who know us know that Julien is autistic and up until recently was for the most part non-verbal. So, for him to greet us the way he did, and then come to each of us and give us hugs was HUGE. It made my heart swell. I had to run to the store, and when I got back, Jess & Chris were here with our other two grandchildren Fiona & Ramsey. Everyone was in the pool. I still had some yard work to do but ya know what….SCREW IT! It’s days like this you don’t get back if you ignore them. Yard work can wait for another day. In the pool I went. When it came time to start cooking dinner (which is usually my job by choice on family Sundays), Karen stepped up and pitched in. She truly is my best friend and best thing in my life. Governor Sherrill, ​As you prepare for your upcoming interview, I am writing to ask that you address the critical financial crisis facing New Jersey’s retired first responders. For those of us who served under the Police and Firemen’s Retirement System (PFRS), the math of retirement simply no longer adds up. ​The Facts: • ​The Broken Promise: When Chapter 78 was signed in 2011, the suspension of the Cost of Living Adjustment (COLA) was presented as a temporary measure to stabilize the fund. Instead, it has been terminated indefinitely, eroding over 35% of our purchasing power while we are told to wait for a target that is decades away. • ​The National Outlier: New Jersey stands alone as the only state in the nation that completely denies a COLA to its retired public servants for this duration. Our first responders didn’t suspend their service when things got difficult, yet their financial security has been suspended for 15 years. • ​The Chapter 78 Burden: While our income remains flat, our expenses are rising. The state continues to approve massive health benefit premium increases, including the 20% plus hikes seen in 2026. This is an unsustainable burden for retirees on fixed incomes who served decades under the promise of stable, earned benefits. • ​A Failed Solution: The 2018 Chapter 55 law was intended to give the PFRS Board the independence to manage its own destiny. Yet, we are still being held to the general pension system’s 80% funding trap, a target that current Treasury projections suggest won’t be reached until 2042. ​My Direct Question for the Governor: ​With New Jersey managing a record $60.7 billion budget, why are our retired first responders still being forced to pay for the state’s historical underfunding through a "temporary" freeze that has lasted 15 years? ​Will you commit to supporting active legislation, specifically S2065/A1168 to restore the COLA, as well as S211/A1685, and any future legislation proposed to restore the COLA and provide broader pension reform to protect the benefits of vested retirees? ​We have done our jobs, Governor. We are asking you to do yours by honoring the contract made with those who spent their lives serving New Jersey. #COLANOW #askgovsherrill https://www.facebook.com/share/p/1GojrLFEzx/

🤍 She was told at 16 she would never carry a child. Last Christmas, she held her son. Grace Davidson was born with MRKH syndrome, a rare condition in which a girl is born without a functioning womb. Diagnosed as a teenager, she grew up believing pregnancy would never be part of her story. Then medicine opened a door. In 2024, at Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, surgeons performed a groundbreaking womb transplant at The Churchill Hospital in Oxford. The donor was a young woman who had died, and whose family made the extraordinary decision to donate. Recovery followed. Then IVF. Then an embryo transfer. Then months of waiting that felt endless. Just before Christmas 2025, baby Hugo Powell was delivered by caesarean section at Queen Charlotte's and Chelsea Hospital. He weighed 6 pounds 13 ounces. He became the first baby in the UK born to a mother who received a womb from a deceased donor. Grace called it a miracle. She has spoken about thinking of the donor’s family every day. In the middle of their own grief, they chose to give another woman the chance to become a mother. Around 5,000 women in the UK are born with MRKH syndrome. For many, pregnancy has never been possible. Hugo’s birth does not change the past. But it changes what the future might hold. Sometimes hope arrives because someone else, in their darkest moment, says yes. #MedicalBreakthrough #OrganDonation #Hope #MRKH #Miracle

RIP Autumn, my beloved friend, companion and cat. I found her in a forest area near the edge of the city about ten years ago. She was orphaned as a kitten. I was taking care of her mother who had disappeared, Autumn and her siblings were left to fend for themselves when they were only half grown. She and her sister Blackball survived and grew to adulthood. They were still feral but I had gained their trust and they would come to me and let me pet them after some time. Autumn was a kind and gentle creature but a warrior born. One night as I was going to feed her, I found her facing off against the largest raccoon I have ever seen. She had kittens of her own at this time and the raccoon had them pinned on a high concrete pedestal. This was no social visit, he meant to kill them. Autumn's ears were pulled back and with tooth and claw she struck at him unfazed at his size and strength, she was prepared to fight to the death to protect her own. Despite her valor however it was a good thing I got there when I did. I drove him away and Autumn rubbed up against my leg when I went to check on her. I decided to bring her home with me and there she has stayed ever since. She was born to sleeping on the grass or rocks of her forest home but I always made sure she had a pillow to sleep on and food to eat without fear of black masked marauders in the night when she came to live with me. I love you Autumn, I will find you when my time comes to cross Bifrost Bridge. Fare well sweet girl.

Grayson Murray Foundation establishes scholarship fund at Hazelden Betty Ford to expand access to addiction treatment. November 27, 2025 RALEIGH, N.C. — More people struggling with addiction will soon have access to life-changing treatment, thanks to a new scholarship fund created in memory of the late PGA TOUR champion Grayson Murray. The Grayson Murray Scholarship Fund, established at the Hazelden Betty Ford Foundation, will help remove financial barriers for adults and young people ready to begin their recovery journey. The foundation’s leaders say this new partnership delivers on one of Grayson’s most heartfelt wishes. “Grayson believed deeply in second chances and in the power of recovery,” said Jeff Maness, president of the Grayson Murray Foundation. “He knew that the decision to seek help is one of the bravest a person can make — and that financial barriers too often stand in the way. This scholarship fund is our way of delivering on Grayson’s own wishes: to help others in need that want to heal.” The fund was first announced at the Grayson Murray Classic, a charity golf tournament that brought together athletes and entertainers to celebrate Grayson’s life and legacy. The Grayson Murray Scholarship Fund will help ensure that no one is denied care because of financial hardship. By covering treatment costs at Hazelden Betty Ford’s adult and youth campuses in Center City and Plymouth, Minnesota, the fund provides real, immediate help for individuals and families ready to begin the journey toward recovery. By expanding access to care, it honors Grayson Murray’s legacy and advances the Foundation’s commitment to compassion, resilience, and hope — with each scholarship representing another life restored and another chance at healing. “When Grayson spoke openly about his struggles with mental health and addiction, he gave hope to countless others. Through this partnership, that hope continues,” Maness said. “We are profoundly grateful to the Grayson Murray Foundation for establishing this scholarship fund in memory of Grayson,” said Ahmed Eid, vice president of the Midwest region at Hazelden Betty Ford. “This generous gift will directly support patients who are seeking hope and healing but face financial barriers to care. We know firsthand of the urgent need to expand access to treatment and to destigmatize mental health and addiction. Grayson’s legacy will live on in the lives transformed through this fund, and we are honored to be part of that story.” Grayson was admired as much for his candor as for his competitive fire on the PGA TOUR. He bravely shared his personal experience with anxiety, depression and addiction before his death in May 2024. After his death, Grayson’s parents, Eric and Terry Murray, launched the Foundation to carry forward his mission — as Grayson himself wrote, to “help the ones that want to be helped but might not have the help they need financially.” Through partnerships like these, the Grayson Murray Foundation continues to build a future where mental health and addiction care are accessible, supported, and destigmatized. GEN Petraeus about our military today... I remember the day I found out I got into West Point. My mom actually showed up in the hallway of my high school and waited for me to get out of class. She was bawling her eyes out and apologizing that she had opened up my admission letter. She wasn't crying because it had been her dream for me to go there. She was crying because she knew how hard I'd worked to get in, how much I wanted to attend, and how much I wanted to be an infantry officer. I was going to get that opportunity. That same day two of my teachers took me aside and essentially told me the following: "David, you're a smart guy. You don't have to join the military. You should go to college, instead." I could easily write a theme defending West Point and the military as I did that day, explaining that USMA is an elite institution, that separate from that it is actually statistically much harder to enlist in the military than it is to get admitted to college, that serving the nation is a challenge that all able-bodied men should at least consider for a host of reasons, but I won't. What I will say is that when a 16 year-old kid is being told that attending West Point is going to be bad for his future then there is a dangerous disconnect in America, and entirely too many Americans have no idea what kind of burdens our military is bearing. In World War II, 11.2% of the nation served in four (4) years. During the Vietnam era, 4.3% served in twelve (12) years. Since 2001, only 0.45% of our population has served in the Global War on Terror. These are unbelievable statistics. Over time, fewer and fewer people have shouldered more and more of the burden and it is only getting worse. Our troops were sent to war in Iraq by a Congress consisting of 10% veterans with only one person having a child in the military. Taxes did not increase to pay for the war. War bonds were not sold. Gas was not regulated. In fact, the average citizen was asked to sacrifice nothing, and has sacrificed nothing unless they have chosen to out of the goodness of their hearts. The only people who have sacrificed are the veterans and their families. The volunteers. The people who swore an oath to defend this nation. You stand there, deployment after deployment and fight on. You've lost relationships, spent years of your lives in extreme conditions, years apart from kids you'll never get back, and beaten your body in a way that even professional athletes don't understand. Then you come home to a nation that doesn't understand. They don't understand suffering. They don't understand sacrifice. They don't understand why we fight for them. They don't understand that bad people exist. They look at you like you're a machine - like something is wrong with you. You are the misguided one - not them. When you get out, you sit in the college classrooms with political science teachers that discount your opinions on Iraq and Afghanistan because YOU WERE THERE and can't understand the macro issues they gathered from books, because of your bias. You watch TV shows where every vet has PTSD and the violent strain at that. Your Congress is debating your benefits, your retirement, and your pay, while they ask you to do more. But the amazing thing about you is that you all know this. You know your country will never pay back what you've given up. You know that the populace at large will never truly understand or appreciate what you have done for them. Hell, you know that in some circles, you will be thought as less than normal for having worn the uniform. But you do it anyway. You do what the greatest men and women of this country have done since 1775. YOU SERVED. Just that decision alone makes you part of an elite group. General David Petraeus West Point Class 1974

MARTIN de ALARCON San Antonio Texas Founder Biography He belonged to a family with a military tradition, which is why in the 1680s he was already in the Spanish army in Flanders and Italy in various campaigns. He also served in North Africa just before being sent to the Viceroyalty of New Spain around 1690. In 1691, Viceroy Count Galve appointed him sergeant major of the Guadalajara militia company, one of the viceroyalty's most important border military posts. Shortly afterward, he was appointed mayor and "war captain" of Jacona and Zamora, both in Michoacán. In the fall of 1696, then-viceroy Juan Ortega y Montáñez promoted him to "war captain" and protector of the Indians of the town of Mazapil. He remained in this position, also serving as an active agent in border pacification, especially in the area surrounding Saltillo. His undeniable reputation and excellent knowledge of dealing with the frontier Indians earned him the appointment on December 9, 1716, by the viceroy Marquis de Valero as commander of the important presidio of San Francisco in the province of Coahuila, as well as the even more important position of governor and captain general of the rapidly expanding frontier province of Texas. In this sense, he was a pioneer in the Spanish policy of territorial expansion to the east, as he was responsible for leading the main effort of conquest, exploitation, and settlement in Texas and Coahuila for more than a decade. While on his way to his new assignment, he had to stop in June 1717 in Saltillo, where, delayed for several months, he attended the investigation that was undertaken against the French Baron of Saint Denis, who, like the Spanish, intended to extend French influence towards the western Gulf of Mexico at the expense of Spanish interests. Saint Denis was one of the architects of the rise in smuggling and the significant increase in the danger posed to the Texas Indians, thanks to the sale of weapons. In April 1718, he was finally able to cross the Rio Grande, finally entering the almost inhospitable and unknown land of Texas: he entered the territory with ten families and seventy-two people. On May 1, 1718, he attended the founding of the San Antonio de Valero mission with Franciscan Father Antonio San Buenaventura y Olivares, and four days later, he founded the nearby presidio of San Antonio de Béjar, which over the decades would become the most important presidio in Texas and its political capital. Most of the families who accompanied him served as the origin of what would become the town of Béjar, a flourishing city over the years. He spent the months of October and November 1718 completing the settlement of old Spanish missions in East Texas, which now bordered French Louisiana far to the east. During these months, he had to combat illegal French smuggling in the area, undoubtedly the Spanish main problem at the time. He returned to San Antonio de Béjar in January 1719 and spent the following months warning the French to withdraw from the East Texas territories, which he considered entirely under Spanish sovereignty. At the end of 1719, his term in Texas ended, and he retired to the viceroyalty's capital. His actions in Texas can be considered the beginning of the true Spanish presence in the region, not only for the founding of San Antonio de Béjar, but primarily for having monitored the eastern border and established a cordon of emission against French interference. The Spanish origin of Texas is therefore closely linked to Alarcón's successful policy.

I lied to a customer this morning. Said it straight to her face. And honestly? I’d do it again tomorrow. I’ve been a mechanic for 30 years. My hands are permanently stained with grease, my back is a roadmap of old injuries, and I run my shop with a simple rule: Fix it right. Charge what it’s worth. No exceptions. At 8 a.m., a beat-up Chevy limped into my lot coughing smoke like it needed last rites. A young woman stepped out — couldn’t have been more than 22 — wearing oversized nursing scrubs and exhaustion in her eyes. In the back seat, a baby slept in a car seat, clutching a tiny teddy bear with one ear missing. “It’s making a weird noise,” she said quietly. “Please… please tell me it’s something small.” I popped the hood. It wasn’t small. It wasn’t even medium. It was a disaster — burst hose, shredded belt, leaking oil, one bad drive away from blowing the engine. “To fix this right,” I told her gently, “you’re looking at about a thousand dollars.” She didn’t cry. She didn’t panic. She just stared at her baby. Then at her phone. Then at the ground. “I start my new job at the nursing home in an hour,” she whispered. “If I’m late… they’ll fire me. I don’t have anything left in my account. I was going to put water in it and just… try.” She gently placed a hand on the hood like she was apologising to the car for being poor. That did it. I swear, sometimes life gives you a moment where doing the right thing isn’t a choice — it’s a responsibility. “Give me your keys,” I said. “I can’t pay you,” she said immediately, panic rising again. “Did I ask you for money?” I replied. She blinked at me, unsure. “The part you need,” I lied smoothly, “is on national backorder. Two weeks minimum. You can’t drive this car.” She looked like she was going to collapse. “Two weeks? How do I—how am I supposed to get to work?” I pulled my truck keys out of my pocket and held them out. “Take mine.” Her jaw dropped. “Sir… that’s your truck.” “I know. Built like a tank. It’ll get you to work and back. Bring it back when your car’s done.” She stared at me like she couldn’t decide whether to cry or hug me. My shop manager looked at me like I’d lost my mind. But I’ve been young and broke. I’ve been terrified of losing a job. I’ve been one bill away from falling apart. So she left safely, in my truck, with her baby strapped in the back. And her old Chevy stayed in my garage. There was no backorder. The hose cost $20. But I didn’t stop there. Every lunch break. Every after-hours minute. Every quiet moment in the shop… I rebuilt that car. Brand new tires. Fixed the belt. Cleaned the engine. Rewired the lights. Replaced the brake pads. Oil change. Detailed the interior. Tuned the engine until it purred like it hadn’t purred in years. By the time I was done, that 15-year-old junker felt like a brand-new ride. Two weeks later, she walked back into the shop, my truck keys in hand. “It drove perfectly,” she said softly. “Thank you. Truly. I’m… nervous to see the bill.” I handed her the invoice. TOTAL: $0.00 PAID IN FULL BY FACTORY WARRANTY RECALL. Another lie. A harmless one. A necessary one. She stared at the paper. Then at the car. Then at me. “But… this isn’t a new car,” she whispered. “There can’t be a recall.” “Ma’am,” I said, pretending to fuss with paperwork, “you questioning my paperwork accuracy?” She laughed through tears — that soft, heartbreaking laugh people make when the world finally gives them a break instead of another burden. “Why would you do all this?” she whispered. I looked at her sleeping baby in her arms. “Because you’re trying,” I said. “And the world doesn’t make it easy for people who are trying.” She hugged me. Tight. One of those hugs you feel in your bones. When she drove away in that bright, reliable Chevy, waving out the window, I stood there a long time… thinking. About how many times I wished someone would help me when I was young. About how much difference a little kindness makes. About how good it feels to make someone feel safe — even for a moment. People often say, “You can’t help everyone.” Maybe not. But you can help someone. And sometimes that someone is exactly who needed it that day. So yes — I lied this morning. I lied to give a young mom a chance. I lied to make sure a baby got to daycare safely. I lied so someone wouldn’t lose the job they desperately needed. And if I had to do it again? I’d lie every single time. Because the kindness we give away… is the only part of us that lasts. 💛 Moral: Be the break in someone’s bad day. Be the yes in their world full of no. These aren’t my words but they are very well said & I wanted to share them…. “We put on this uniform without ever asking which day will be the last. We walk through terminals as if time is endless—never knowing when it will be the final boarding, the last laugh on the jumpseat, the last story shared somewhere above the clouds. The smallest moments never feel like goodbyes… until they are. A plastic cup handed to a child. A quiet smile to a stranger. A routine flight that was never meant to be anything more than ordinary. We leave home believing we’ll return— never imagining that, somewhere across the world, a phone will ring… and a family’s life will be forever divided into before and after. A voice on the other end delivering the words no one is ever ready to hear: they’re not coming home this time. Tonight, my heart carries the weight of every life touched by the tragedy of Air Canada Flight 8646— the crew, the passengers, air traffic control, the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey staff, and the families now left to hold what remains. There are no right words for a loss like this—only silence, grief, and remembrance. May your final journey be gentle. May the skies hold you softly. May you be carried home on endless tailwinds. We may wear different uniforms… but this pain, this love, this bond—we all share it. Forever #UnitedByWings”

Can’t take credit for this but it is spot on! Life of a Flight Attendant: We never say I'm flying to London , we say I HAVE London! We trade too, and say things like "Who wants Istanbul? I need Dubai”…Yes, like we own the whole damn world! We drink soup from paper cups like it's coffee in the middle of the night, we use military time to set our alarm, we can finish a meal in 30 seconds standing up...behind a curtain & in between meal service & clearance. We hate when you stand up after the plane lands, we laugh when you clap after the plane lands. We love when you thank us. Aircraft is for Flight Attendants, Airplane is for passengers. We talk in dates even if it’s just the next day. We never know what day it is but we remember what supermarket is closest to our hotel. We are the best packers and can find anything we see in a magazine in the world, clothes, furniture,the best restaurants, best hotels, sightseeing excursions, etc... We may especially have loved working with someone specifically without knowing that person's name or if we will ever fly together again. “4L” or “1R” may be our names for the day. We all have woken up in the middle of the night with a mini heart attack forgetting where we are. We see beautiful places but no one to share the moment with. We are always, always alone in a crowd… #UnitedByWings

What has been most difficult is not just the shooting itself, but the lack of visible community support afterward. Support matters. A phone call matters. A visit matters. A public statement matters. Asking, "How can we help?" matters. When a nonprofit organization serving families, children, seniors, veterans, and individuals experiencing housing instability is impacted by violence, the community should come together. Support from town officials, community leaders, businesses, churches, civic organizations, and residents can make a tremendous difference. Support is not about money. It is about showing up. It is about letting those affected know they are not alone. It is about advocating for justice, sharing information, checking in on victims, and standing united against violence. In times of tragedy, people should not have to ask their community to care. The community should care enough to show up on its own. That is the support we needed. That is the support we still need.

I am a person of reason and empathy, which is why I find it difficult to understand what happened after our transitional home— Sage and Sweetgrass at the Bradshaw House Inc. , the only program of its kind in Ahoskie—was riddled with bullets and our beloved 5-year-old American Bully, Dior, was killed by a stray bullet. The Ahoskie Police Department responded, and for that we are grateful. However, I believe that when a tragedy impacts a family, a nonprofit organization, or a business in our community, town leaders should rally around those affected and show support. It should not be the responsibility of the victim to make phone calls explaining what happened or asking for help. There should be follow-up visits, advocacy, and outreach. Community leaders should check on those impacted, offer resources, and help ensure their voices are heard. I also believe incidents of this magnitude deserve broader awareness. Media outlets should be notified, public officials should speak out against the violence, and social media should be used to keep the community informed and engaged. When gun violence strikes a home filled with families, children, and vulnerable individuals, and a life is lost—even the life of a beloved family pet—it should matter to the entire community. Communities grow stronger when they stand together, not just during celebrations, but also during moments of tragedy. We are still seeking accountability for the June 13, 2026 shooting at Sage & Sweetgrass at the Bradshaw House Inc. We remain committed to our mission of housing hope, not violence, and we hope our community will continue to stand with us as we seek justice for Dior and safety for all.
